title: Riesling around the world
subtitle: Germany, Alsace, Austria, Australia
objectives: Explain why Riesling expresses place clearly

steps.title: Germany
steps.body: Riesling is Germany's great grape. In the cool Mosel, on steep slate slopes, it gives light wines, often 7.5 to 9% alcohol, with high acidity and some sweetness. In the Rheingau and Pfalz, warmer and broader, it gives fuller, more often dry wines. Labels may use Prädikat terms, like Kabinett or Spätlese, for ripeness at harvest.

steps.title: Why Riesling shows place
steps.body: Riesling is rarely oaked, rarely put through malolactic, and is almost never blended. With nothing to mask it, the vineyard speaks clearly: slate, granite and limestone sites give recognisably different wines. Its high acidity, often above 8 g/l, also keeps it fresh for decades, from dry to sweet.
steps.highlight: No oak, no blend: pure place

steps.prompt: Most German Riesling labelled Kabinett is fermented in new oak.
steps.explanation: Not true. Riesling is almost always made without new oak, to keep its pure fruit and acidity. Kabinett refers to ripeness at harvest, not winemaking.

steps.title: Alsace, Austria, Australia
steps.body: In Alsace, Riesling is mostly dry, fuller and riper, from a dry, sunny valley sheltered by the Vosges. Austria's Wachau and Kamptal make dry, powerful versions on steep terraces above the Danube. Australia's Clare and Eden Valleys give dry, lime-scented wines that develop toast and petrol notes with age.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Riesling.
steps.explanation: Each place gives a distinct style, from light and off-dry to powerful and dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Germany's Mosel gives light, high-acid, often off-dry Riesling
Alsace, Austria and Australia make mostly dry Riesling
Riesling shows place clearly because it's rarely oaked or blended
